description: Water heater step() logic: electric resistance, gas burner, config validation, and thermal stratification interaction.

reviews.title: Electric resistance WH step(): heating element, thermostat, energy accounting
reviews.prompt: Electric resistance water heater step() implements the most common US WH type (present in ~40% of residences). Review each substep: (a) Heating element control: one or two elements (upper + lower). In a two-element non-simultaneous WH, the upper element has priority and the lower element only energizes when the upper thermostat is satisfied. Verify this interlock logic is correct—simultaneous operation of both elements would draw double the rated power (typically 4.5 kW each = 9 kW total) and would trip a 30A residential circuit. (b) Thermostat logic: each element has its own thermostat with setpoint and deadband. Upper thermostat setpoint is typically 5-10°F above lower to ensure upper element priority. Verify the deadband prevents short-cycling: typical deadband is 5-10°F (2.8-5.6°C). Element turns on when T < setpoint - deadband/2, off when T > setpoint + deadband/2. (c) Energy accounting: electrical energy consumed = element_power * timestep * on_fraction. Verify this energy is correctly accounted in the building electrical balance and in the thermal balance as heat added to the tank. (d) Tank stratification: verify the resistance model correctly interacts with the tank node model—the upper element heats the top node, the lower element heats a lower node. Natural buoyancy moves heated water upward; verify the model captures this stratification or documents the mixed-tank assumption. (e) Parasitic losses: verify tank jacket losses (UA) are computed and applied to the correct tank nodes (typically distributed proportionally to node surface area).

reviews.title: Gas WH step(): burner efficiency, UEF/EF, pilot consumption, flue losses
reviews.prompt: Gas water heater step() implements gas-fired storage water heaters. Review: (a) Burner efficiency: gas WHs have rated combustion efficiency (typically 0.76-0.96 EF/UEF). Verify that the combustion efficiency is applied correctly—fuel energy * efficiency = heat delivered to water. The remaining (1-efficiency) * fuel energy is lost as flue gas sensible and latent heat. A common error is applying efficiency to the electrical side (double-counting) or omitting flue losses from the thermal balance. (b) UEF/EF handling: understand the difference between Energy Factor (EF, pre-2015 test procedure) and Uniform Energy Factor (UEF, post-2015). UEF values are typically lower than EF for the same WH. Verify which metric the model uses and whether a conversion is applied. EF/UEF includes standby losses (jacket losses, pilot) and cycling losses (purge, distribution). If the model splits recovery efficiency from standby losses, verify the split is physically correct and their sum equals the EF/UEF. (c) Standing pilot consumption: gas WHs with standing pilots consume 200-800 BTU/h (60-230 W equivalent) continuously. Verify this consumption is modeled as heat input to the tank (not lost) during standby and as additional fuel consumption. (d) Flue loss routing to zone: in winter, flue losses from a WH located in conditioned space contribute to space heating (reducing furnace load). In summer, these losses increase cooling load. Verify the flue loss fraction is routed to the correct thermal zone—typically, the WH is in the basement/garage, and flue losses to that zone are calculated. (e) Condensing vs non-condensing: condensing gas WHs (UEF > 0.90) extract latent heat from flue gases. Verify the model handles the condensation heat recovery correctly (additional ~8-10% of fuel energy recovered from water vapor latent heat).

reviews.title: WH config struct: tank volume, UA, setpoint, deadband — no impossible combos
reviews.prompt: WH Config struct validation for all fields. Verify no physically impossible combinations are allowed: (a) tank_volume_l: must be > 0 and ≤ 500 L (residential range is 80-450 L, with 190 L / 50 gal being most common). A zero-volume tank would have infinite temperature response; a negative volume is unphysical. (b) ua_w_per_k: jacket heat loss coefficient. Must be > 0 (a perfectly insulated tank with UA=0 would violate the Second Law as it could theoretically store heat indefinitely). Typical values: for a 190L tank with R-12 to R-24 insulation, UA = surface_area / R_value ≈ 2.5 m² / (12 * 0.176 m²·K/W) ≈ 1.2 W/K for R-12, or ≈ 0.6 W/K for R-24. Verify default UA is in this range and scales with tank surface area (larger tanks have proportionally higher UA). (c) setpoint_c: must be in safe range, typically 49-60°C (120-140°F). Below 49°C risks Legionella growth; above 60°C risks scalding. Verify the default (typically 51.7°C / 125°F) is within this range. (d) deadband_c: must be > 0 and typically 2.8-5.6°C (5-10°F). A deadband of 0 would cause infinite switching frequency. Verify the deadband is symmetric around the setpoint. (e) Element power rating: typically 3.0-5.5 kW for residential elements at 240V. Two elements should not sum to more than 30A * 240V = 7.2 kW for the circuit (or the non-simultaneous interlock must be enforced). (f) Check for field interactions: tank volume and UA should be positively correlated (bigger tank = higher UA). If a small volume has a very high UA (or vice versa), the WH will behave non-physically—recovering heat loss instantly or taking days to cool down. Add cross-field validation or warning.
